response.response:
{
  "research_question": "How do five distinct stimulation paradigms (Combined, ICMS Only, Dim Visual Only, Bright Visual Only, and Sham) affect mouse navigation performance metrics including Time-to-Target, Success, Path Efficiency, Average Speed, and Angular Dispersion (AD)?",
  "stim_paradigms_compared": [
    "Combined",
    "ICMS Only",
    "Dim Visual Only",
    "Bright Visual Only",
    "Sham"
  ],
  "response_variables": [
    "Time-to-Target",
    "Success",
    "Path Efficiency",
    "Average Speed",
    "AD"
  ],
  "descriptive_findings": [
    "The Combined paradigm yielded the highest success rate (0.7798) and the fastest mean Time-to-Target (2.56 seconds) among all groups.",
    "The Sham group exhibited the lowest success rate (0.2733) and the slowest mean Time-to-Target (4.68 seconds), indicating significant impairment compared to other conditions.",
    "Path Efficiency was highest in the Bright Visual Only group (0.5036), followed closely by the Combined group (0.5022), while the Sham group had the lowest efficiency (0.3084).",
    "Average Speed was highest in the Combined group (12.83) and lowest in the Sham group (10.74), though differences were less pronounced than in success or time metrics.",
    "Angular Dispersion (AD) was highest in the Combined group (0.3994) and lowest in the Sham group (0.2360), suggesting that while Combined stimulation may increase path variability, it does so within a context of higher overall success."
  ],
  "strongest_group_differences": [
    "The most striking difference is in the Success metric, where the Sham group (0.2733) performs substantially worse than the Combined (0.7798), ICMS Only (0.6854), and Dim Visual Only (0.6733) groups.",
    "Time-to-Target shows a large gap between the Sham group (4.68s) and the Combined group (2.56s), with the Sham group taking nearly twice as long to reach the target on average.",
    "Path Efficiency displays a clear hierarchy where the Sham group (0.3084) is significantly less efficient than all stimulation groups, which cluster between 0.43 and 0.50.",
    "The Dim Visual Only group shows a notably lower success rate (0.6733) compared to the Combined and ICMS Only groups, suggesting that visual stimulation alone is less effective than combined or purely electrical stimulation."
  ],
  "practical_interpretation": "Stimulation paradigms significantly alter navigation outcomes. The Combined paradigm appears most effective, balancing high success rates with rapid target acquisition. The Sham condition represents a baseline of severe impairment, particularly in task completion (Success) and route efficiency. While the Combined group shows higher angular dispersion, this is likely a byproduct of the increased speed and success rather than a failure of navigation, as the group still achieves targets faster and more often than any other condition.",
  "limitations": [
    "The analysis relies solely on summary statistics (mean, SD, n) provided in the artifacts; individual subject-level data is not available to assess variance within groups or perform statistical significance testing.",
    "The dataset is heavily imbalanced, with the Combined group comprising 48,846 rows (63.7%) of the data, while the Sham group has only 3,505 rows (4.6%), which may skew the overall means and limit the generalizability of findings for the Sham condition.",
    "Missingness is reported as zero for all variables, but the impact of the row filters on the representativeness of the 'Sham' group relative to the others is unknown.",
    "No information is provided regarding the specific nature of the 'Combined' stimulation (e.g., ratio of visual to ICMS) or the specific parameters of the ICMS, limiting mechanistic interpretation."
  ],
  "recommended_next_analysis": "Conduct an ANOVA or Kruskal-Wallis test on each of the five response variables to determine if the observed mean differences between the five stimulation paradigms are statistically significant, followed by post-hoc pairwise comparisons (e.g., Tukey's HSD) to identify specific group differences."
}
